source.title: Codebook Capacity Governs Perceptual Quality Across Resolutions in Hierarchical Discrete Video Compression

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper cites language-model scaling laws as background but does not test or rely on the claim about language-model pretraining loss or compute-optimal allocation. Its experiments concern perceptual quality in video compression.
record.gate_note: The paper reports a log-linear fit and LPIPS measurements for video codecs, not held-out language-model cross-entropy, parameter/token/compute scaling, downstream task performance, or compute-optimal allocation. Those video-compression results are recorded as related findings under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The paper cites Kaplan et al. only as background. Its experiments sweep VQ codebook size K and spatial resolution in a video codec and measure LPIPS. That is not loss versus parameters, tokens or compute, so no version is tested. The fit is linear in log2 K, not a power law in model or data scale. V5 is therefore not tested either: K is a rate-capacity knob and LPIPS is a distortion metric, not training loss.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct. The authors also report three further results. Bottom-level entropy efficiency rises with resolution (84–87% at 64×64, 92–94% at 256×256). Their codec beats H.264 (25–52% lower LPIPS at 128×128) and H.265 (21–37% at 256×256) at matched or lower bitrate. They argue that discrete codecs are more resolution-stable than continuous-latent ones.
record.recipe_differences: A video-compression sweep varying codebook capacity and spatial resolution, with LPIPS as the outcome; it does not use the language-model loss-scaling method.

fits_no_version.finding: In MS-VQ-VAE video compression on 500 UCF101 test clips, an OLS fit of LPIPS on log2 K and log2 resolution over 12 points gave α=−0.0094 (p<0.001), β=−0.0009 (p=0.68) and R2=0.82. LPIPS falls monotonically with K at every resolution.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In a hierarchical discrete video codec, perceptual distortion falls roughly log-linearly with codebook capacity and shows no significant dependence on resolution from 64 to 256 px.

record.peer_reviewed: NeurIPS 2026, Track on Evaluations and Datasets (as stated in the paper)
record.problems: The experiments concern video-codec LPIPS rather than any specified language-model scaling measure, so they do not provide evidence on the claim versions. The paper also identifies a single dataset and a limited resolution range as limitations.
record.verdict_notes: The record's rows are accurate against Table 2 and Section 5.2, and linking them to no version is correct. Entropy-efficiency (Table 3) and codec-comparison results are not recorded as rows, but they bear on no version, so they are not listed as missing. The paper does call its fit an 'empirical scaling law', but the scaled variable is codebook size, not model, data or compute scale.

versions.untested_parts: Not tested: language-model held-out pretraining loss versus parameter count, tokens, or compute.
Not tested: predictions from small language-model runs against much larger runs.
Not tested: compute-optimal parameter and token allocation.
Not tested: effects of language-model depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.

Although the study concerns video, it measures LPIPS in a discrete video codec as a function of codebook capacity and resolution, not the claimed power-law form for pretraining loss across modalities or training regimes.
Not tested: downstream language-model task performance or its relation to pretraining loss.
Not tested: fitting choices or setup dependence of the specified language-model scaling laws.

rows.uncertainty: α: standard error 0.0014, t=−6.55, p<0.001; β: standard error 0.0020, t=−0.43, p=0.68
